primary.title: Real dance organs, built in Herentals

intro.text: Decap Herentals builds dance organs: organs made for people to dance to, with dynamics and volume control no mechanical organ has. Start from our proven modules or have every detail made for you. Pipes, digital sound or both, with the front instruments Decap organs have carried since 1933. Decap organs play all over the world, from Japan to the US and Australia.

primary.title: Dance organs first

body.text: Dance organs

What we normally build. Between 1960 and 1980 some 120 dance cafés and dance halls across Belgium each had a dance organ, and people came to dance every day. Today Decap dance organs play in living rooms, cafés and dance halls, and on stage: their sensitivity and volume are controllable, so they fit the room instead of filling it. That is why Guido Belcanto could tour one in his theatre show Balzaal der Gebroken Harten in 2008.
Street and fair organs
We have built them, and we can build one for you, but they are the exception in our workshop.
Church and concert organs
In 2025 we built smARTvalve into the first transportable church organ, with every pipe controlled on its own. That organ is L'Explorateur, the mobile concert organ of Swiss organist Yves Rechsteiner.

primary.statement: The first orchestrions were built to sound like a real orchestra. In the golden age of the dance organ, everyone stopped trying. *We never did.*

caption.text: In the 19th century makers such as Limonaire and Wurlitzer worked to bring their mechanical orchestras closer to real musicians, who play with feeling and nuance. When people came to love the mechanical sound itself, that work stopped. We are musicians first, so for the last 50 years we kept going: organs that play with feeling and nuance, from the living room to the stage.

primary.title: Every instrument its own part

intro.text: We were the first to put an organ on MIDI. Most organs now use MIDI to replace the book, and nothing more. A Decap organ uses all of it: every instrument group gets its own part, with soft and hard notes.

primary.book_caption: The book decides. Instruments coupled to the same track follow the same line, and every note sounds at the same strength.
primary.decap_caption: Every instrument group has its own MIDI address and its own part: the saxophone plays the melody, the violins a counter-melody, the piano soft and hard.
primary.note: Example arrangement. Note height and brightness show how hard each note is played.

items.title: 256 separate addresses
items.body: 16 ports of 16 channels each. Every instrument group gets its own address, so an arranger can write a real part for each one.

items.title: Soft or hard, per note
items.body: On a traditional organ the drumstick always hits with the same force. On a Decap organ it hits soft or hard, with adjustable timing.

items.title: Wind pressure per chest
items.body: Different intensities per wind chest, and ranks that play vibrato.

items.title: A processor behind every part
items.body: No air-driven mechanism: every drum, valve and register is controlled digitally. That is what makes soft and hard notes, wind control and volume control possible.

items.title: Volume you control
items.body: Soft in a living room, full in a theatre, loud enough for a DJ set.

items.title: smARTvalve: every pipe its own wind
items.body: Our newest development takes wind control down to every single pipe.

items.title: All software, our own
items.body: The CNC programs that mill our pipes, the software that drives the organ and the Virtual Orchestrion player: all developed in Herentals.

intro.text: Processors and chips control every part of a Decap organ. That is what lets it play soft and hard, change its wind and fit any room.

intro.text: In 1977 François Decap built the first digital dance organ, so dance halls and cafés with much smaller budgets could have an organ. Today you choose the mix.

primary.title: Accordions on Decap organs since 1933

body.text: The year Frans Decap founded Decap Herentals, the first self-playing accordions appeared on Decap organs. They still do. A Decap organ front can carry:
a real accordion, played by the organ
a drum kit
percussion such as woodblock, tambourine and cowbell
animated figures
We make these instruments as stand-alone self-playing instruments too, so every one is proven on its own before it goes into an organ. See our instruments.

primary.title: A 105-key organ that also plays 121-key music

body.text: Our standard scales are 105 and 121 keys, but the scale does not have to limit your repertoire. Every new Decap organ comes with our Virtual Orchestrion player. When an arrangement calls for ranks your organ does not have, the player adds them virtually, with samples we recorded in our own workshop and VST instruments.

Since 2000 a Decap organ plays its music from one digital card instead of racks of cardboard books. If you miss the book, the player projects it on screen while the organ plays. Choose the organ that fits your room and budget, not the one that fits your music.

primary.image_brief: Virtual Orchestrion running on a touchscreen beside an organ, the animated book view visible on screen; 4:3

primary.title: Expression on every pipe

body.text: We have set the wind pressure per wind chest for years. smARTvalve does it per pipe: a valve with its own sensor and processor for every pipe, correcting the pressure 2,000 times a second. Each pipe can play from silence up to four times its voiced pressure, with its own wind envelope and two vibratos, all over MIDI.
It is the technology in the 2025 transportable church organ, the first organ we call a wind synthesizer.

intro.text: Five steps, and you see your organ before we build it.

items.question: What does a new organ cost?

answer.text: Every organ is quoted on its own, because the price follows your choices: the size, pipes or digital sound, the front instruments, the façade. A digital or modular organ costs less than a bespoke pipe organ, and you can reuse pipes or instruments you already have. Send us your starting point and we reply with a first idea and a quote.

items.question: Do you also build street organs and fair organs?

answer.text: Yes, we have built them and can build one for you. But what we normally build are real dance organs, with the dynamic percussion, wind control and volume control that make them play in living rooms and on stage as well as in dance halls.

items.question: What is the difference between 105 and 121 keys?

answer.text: The number of keys sets how many notes and ranks the organ has, and so which music it plays as written. With our Virtual Orchestrion player a 105-key organ also plays 121-key music: missing ranks are added virtually.

items.question: Should I choose pipes or digital sound?

answer.text: Pipes give the real sound of wind in wood. Digital sound needs less space and a smaller budget. Pipes and digital combined sit in between. Tell us about the room and the music, and we advise.

items.question: Where does the music come from?

answer.text: From a digital card in the Virtual Orchestrion player: a whole music library instead of racks of books. Copy-protected arrangements in our shop are coming soon. You can also play the organ live over MIDI.

items.question: Do you deliver organs outside Belgium?

answer.text: Yes. Decap organs play all over the world: in Japan, the US, Australia, Asia and across Europe. Shipping and installation are part of the quote and depend on the project. Warranty is always included.

items.question: Can you restore my old organ or add MIDI to it?

answer.text: Restoration is done by Atelier Frank Decap, Tony's brother. Our MIDI conversion units add MIDI to book and roll organs while the book or roll keeps working.

items.question: Are you the same company as Gebroeders Decap in Antwerp?

answer.text: No. Both descend from the same founder, Aloïs Decap. Decap Herentals was founded by his son Frans in 1933 and is run today by Tony Decap. The two companies are independent and on friendly terms.
